\section[\texorpdfstring{\te{కోరు} (kōru)}{కోరు (kōru)}]{\te{కోరు} (kōru) — to wish for, to ask for}

\label{lesson:TE-C108-koru}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for an intention, then the Telugu for a plan.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కోరు}}
\textbf{\te{కోరు}} — \emph{kōru} — \textquotedblleft{}to wish for, to ask for\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{కోరు}} (\emph{kōru}) is native Dravidian, one word with Tamil \emph{kōru} and Kannada \emph{kōru} (DEDR 2232). DEDR lists Telugu \emph{kōru}, \textquotedblleft{}to desire, request\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Telugu for an intention, then the Telugu for a plan, then say \emph{kōru} again
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\te{అందువల్ల}} (\emph{anduvalla}) is native Dravidian: \emph{andu}, \textquotedblleft{}there, that\textquotedblright{}, on the far-pointing base of DEDR 1, and \emph{valla}, \textquotedblleft{}because of\textquotedblright{}, which DEDR 5276 lists as the postposition \emph{valana}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వల్ల}}
